# Welcome {#welcome .unnumbered}

::: {.tada-hero}
<p class="tada-eyebrow">Best practice for code sharing</p>

## Your analysis should still run when someone else opens it. {.unlisted .unnumbered}

Most published analytical code is never shared. When it *is* shared, it very
often does not run. This wiki is about closing that gap with four things you
can do in an afternoon.
:::

## What this wiki is {.unnumbered}

Sharing code is essential for transparency and computational reproducibility,
and journal policies increasingly require it. But the proportion of papers in
ecology and evolutionary biology with open code remains low — reported rates
range from roughly **5% to 33%** — and lags far behind open data. Worse, code
that *is* shared often does not work: in one review of over 9,000 R files
archived in the Harvard Dataverse, **74% failed to complete without error**,
falling only to **56%** after automated cleaning (removing local file paths,
fixing library installation and loading). In a study of species distribution
and abundance papers, the authors had to abandon their reproducibility
assessment because **93% of scripts** did not run, or ran with errors.

A major reason is simply not knowing how to archive analytical code properly.
Existing resources tend to be written for *software developers* rather than for
researchers writing a one-off analysis for one dataset.

**TADA** — Transferable, Available, Documented, Annotated — is a set of simple
guidelines aimed exactly at that gap. This wiki turns TADA into a working
reference, and surrounds it with the related practices you need: metadata,
licences, repository choice, the SORTEE data and code quality control
guidelines, and code review.

## TADA in four cards {.unnumbered}

::: {.tada-cards}
::: {.tada-card .t}
[T]{.tada-letter} [Transferable]{.tada-word}
[Anyone can open your file and run it, on their machine, without converting or
editing it first.]{.tada-gloss}
:::

::: {.tada-card .a1}
[A]{.tada-letter} [Available]{.tada-word}
[The code is publicly archived somewhere immutable, with a persistent
identifier (a DOI) that is cited in the paper.]{.tada-gloss}
:::

::: {.tada-card .d}
[D]{.tada-letter} [Documented]{.tada-word}
[A README describes the files, the software environment, the licence, and
where the data live.]{.tada-gloss}
:::

::: {.tada-card .a2}
[A]{.tada-letter} [Annotated]{.tada-word}
[Comments inside the code say what each chunk does, why, and which result in
the paper it produces.]{.tada-gloss}
:::
:::

::: {.tada-key}
TADA is deliberately a **minimum standard**, not a counsel of perfection.
Analytical code is usually tailored to one dataset and one study — its job is
to be a transparent, reproducible record of that analysis, not to become
reusable software. TADA sets the bar where it needs to be for that job, and
maps onto the FAIR principles while it does so.
:::

## How to use this wiki {.unnumbered}

| If you want to… | Go to |
|---|---|
| Get code ready to submit, today | [Start here](#quickstart) |
| Understand TADA and how it maps to FAIR | [TADA at a glance](#tada) |
| Work through one principle at a time | [Transferable](#transferable), [Available](#available), [Documented](#documented), [Annotated](#annotated) |
| Write a README, pick a licence, choose a repository | [Data & code sharing](#data-sharing) |
| Know what a journal data editor will check | [The SORTEE guidelines](#sortee) |
| Set up or run a code review | [Code review](#code-review) |
| Find guides, tutorials and papers | [Further reading](#further-reading) |
| Add a page to this wiki | [Contribute](#contribute) |

Each chapter is self-contained, so it is fine to arrive from a search and read
only the section you need. Cross-references point to the rest.

## Who this is for {.unnumbered}

Researchers at **any** level of coding experience who need to share the code
behind a paper. The examples use R and Python, because those are the languages
most used in ecology and evolutionary biology, but the principles apply to
workflow languages (e.g. Snakemake) and compiled languages (e.g. C++) too, and
to disciplines well beyond ecology.

You do **not** need to know Git, Docker or unit testing to follow this wiki.
Those tools appear where they genuinely help, and are always marked as
optional extras rather than requirements.

## Where the guidance comes from {.unnumbered}

This wiki is a synthesis of three sources, all of which are worth reading in
full. Copies, and their terms of use, are in
[`papers/`](papers/README.md).

- **Ivimey-Cook, E. R., Culina, A., Dimri, S., Grainger, M. J., Kar, F.,
  Lagisz, M., Moran, N. P., Nakagawa, S., Roche, D. G., Tattan, S.,
  Sánchez-Tójar, A., Windecker, S. M., & Pick, J. L.** *TADA! Simple guidelines
  to improve analytical code sharing for transparency and reproducibility.*
  → the four TADA principles, and the [Transferable](#transferable),
  [Available](#available), [Documented](#documented) and
  [Annotated](#annotated) chapters.

- **Pick, J. L., Allen, B. J., Bachelot, B., Bairos-Novak, K. R., Brand, J. A.,
  Class, B., Dallas, T., D'Amelio, P. B., Fenollosa, E., Fernández-Juricic, E.,
  Gomes, D. G. E., Grainger, M. J., Guillemaud, T., John, C., Krasnow, R.,
  Lagisz, M., Lequime, S., Maynard, D. S., Nakagawa, S., O'Dea, R. E.,
  Paquet, M., Petitjean, Q., Sánchez-Tójar, A., van Dis, N. E., Wilson, L. A. B.,
  & Ivimey-Cook, E. R. (2026).** *The SORTEE guidelines for data and code
  quality control in ecology and evolutionary biology.* **Peer Community
  Journal 6: e20.** <https://doi.org/10.24072/pcjournal.687>
  → the [SORTEE guidelines](#sortee) section and most of
  [Data & code sharing](#data-sharing).

- **Ivimey-Cook, E. R., Pick, J. L., Bairos-Novak, K. R., Culina, A.,
  Gould, E., Grainger, M., Marshall, B. M., Moreau, D., Paquet, M.,
  Royauté, R., Sánchez-Tójar, A., Silva, I., & Windecker, S. M. (2023).**
  *Implementing code review in the scientific workflow: Insights from ecology
  and evolutionary biology.* **Journal of Evolutionary Biology 36: 1347–1356.**
  <https://doi.org/10.1111/jeb.14230>
  → the [Code review](#code-review) chapter.

Full details, plus everything else cited, are in [References](#references).

::: {.tada-note}
Where this wiki adds practical detail that goes beyond the source papers — a
worked README, a repository comparison table, a reviewer script — it is marked
as **wiki guidance** rather than presented as a finding from the papers.
:::

## Building this wiki {.unnumbered}

```bash
Rscript render.R
```

The rendered site lands in `docs/`. See [Contribute](#contribute) for the file
layout, the page template, and how to add a chapter.
